abstract: Cerebrospinal fluid-contacting neurons (CSF-cNs) are an evolutionarily conserved population of spinal sensory neurons positioned around the central canal and characterized by expression of the ion channel PKD2L1. CSF-cNs contribute to locomotor control, but little is known about variation in this sensory system among commonly used laboratory mouse populations. We compared motor performance and CSF-cN organization in closely related C57BL/6 mice obtained from The Jackson Laboratory (Jackson), Charles River Laboratories (Charles River), and Taconic Biosciences (Taconic). Motor performance differed among suppliers, with Charles River mice performing better than Taconic mice on balance beam and rotarod tasks, whereas grid walking performance did not differ significantly among groups. CSF-cN organization also differed significantly among suppliers. Jackson mice had the greatest abundance of PKD2L1+ cells and canal-contacting cells, and a greater proportion of PKD2L1+ cells contacted the central canal in Jackson mice than in Charles River or Taconic mice. CSF-cNs were also more abundant in cervical than lumbar spinal cord regions, whereas the proportion contacting the canal showed only a trend toward a regional difference. Individual CSF-cN measures did not show significant associations with motor performance. These findings demonstrate significant supplier-associated variation in both motor performance and the organization of the CSF-cN anatomy and show that greater CSF-cN abundance does not necessarily correspond to better motor performance.
